cues.text: Ascension Day on the Volcano's Slope

On the morning of May 8, 1902, the feast of the Ascension, Mount Pelee, the volcano towering over the French Caribbean island of Martinique, erupted violently, sending lava and ash pouring down its slopes.

The flow reached the port city of Saint-Pierre almost immediately, destroying it completely and killing nearly all of its roughly 28,000 residents within minutes — one of the deadliest volcanic disasters of the twentieth century.
A Village Turns to the Altar
Five kilometers away, on the volcano's own slopes, the village of Morne-Rouge — long known for its devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus — watched the catastrophe unfold.
Rather than flee, villagers hurried to their parish church, appealing first to Our Lady of Deliverance, the village's own patroness, to spare them.
Father Mary, the parish priest, gave general absolution, distributed Holy Communion, and exposed the Blessed Sacrament for adoration.
The Sacred Heart in the Host
As the congregation prayed before the exposed Host, a woman cried out that she could see the Sacred Heart of Jesus, crowned with thorns, within it.
A large number of those present reported witnessing the same image, and some described seeing blood dripping from the Heart itself.
The vision continued for several hours, ending only when the Blessed Sacrament was returned to the tabernacle.
Spared, Then Lost
Morne-Rouge itself was spared that day, even as Saint-Pierre lay in ruins nearby, and the village's survival gave the congregation's prayers a weight no later retelling has needed to embellish.

But the reprieve proved temporary: on August 30 of that same year, a second eruption of Mount Pelee struck Morne-Rouge directly, destroying the village and killing most of those who had witnessed the vision months before.
Legacy
The Morne-Rouge account is unusual among Eucharistic traditions for ending not in triumph but in loss.
The very community spared by one eruption was destroyed by the next, a fact the tradition has never tried to soften or explain away.
What endures from that Ascension Day is not a claim that faith secured permanent safety, but a witness to what the people of Morne-Rouge chose to do.
With the little time they had left, they did not scatter in panic, but gathered, confessed, received Communion, and knelt together before the Sacrament.
They did so in the shadow of the mountain that would, within the year, take nearly all of them.
